Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 99, verse 1:

Surat az-Zalzalah (The Earthquake)

It is also said: "Surah idha zulzilat" (the surah of "When the earth quakes"). It is Meccan according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ata', and Madinan according to Qatadah and Muqatil.

In al-Itqan (al-Suyuti's 'Ulum al-Qur'an), evidence is cited for the claim that it is Madinan from what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When the verse ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ was revealed, etc., I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, will I be seen in my deeds?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'Those are the great ones, the great ones?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'The small ones, the small ones?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'Woe to my mother!' He said: 'Rejoice, O Abu Sa'id, for a good deed is rewarded tenfold.'" The hadith continues.

Abu Sa'id was only in Madinah, and he did not reach maturity until after Uhud. Its verses number eight in the Kufan and the first Madinan (reckoning), and nine in the rest.

It is authentically reported in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi, al-Bayhaqi and others, from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the earthquake (al-Zalzalah) is recited, it equals half the Qur'an."

Another hadith describes it as a quarter (of the Qur'an). The explanation of the first is that the rulings of the Qur'an are divided into rulings of this world and rulings of the Hereafter, and this surah comprises the rulings of the Hereafter in summary, and it surpasses al-Qari'ah in mentioning the bringing forth of burdens and the reports of news. The explanation of the second is that faith in the Resurrection, which this surah establishes, is a quarter of faith.

In the hadith narrated by al-Tirmidhi: "A servant does not believe until he believes in four things: he testifies that there is no god but Allah, and that I am the Messenger of Allah, sent with the truth; he believes in death; he believes in resurrection after death; and he believes in predestination (al-qadar)."

What relates to this subject will come, Allah willing. It seems that when He, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned in the preceding surah the recompense of the two groups, the believers and the disbelievers, this acted as a prompt to ask about its time, so He, glorified be His majesty, explained it in this surah, and so the Mighty Speaker said:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿When the earth is shaken﴾, i.e., it is moved with a violent, continuous, repeated motion.

﴿Its earthquake﴾, i.e., the particular earthquake belonging to it, which is required by the divine will according to the wisdom-based arrangement; it is the severe earthquake after which there is no other earthquake, so that whatever else is compared to it is not considered an earthquake; or "its wondrous earthquake" whose extent cannot be measured. The idafah (annexation) in both cases is for definiteness (al-'ahd). It is also permissible that it signify totality (al-istighraq), since zilzal is a verbal noun (masdar) in annexation and thus generalizes, i.e., "its whole earthquake"; this is conventional totality intended for emphasis, and it is the meaning of one who said "i.e., its earthquake that falls within the realm of possibility," or he intended by it definiteness as well. Al-Jahdari and 'Isa read "zalzalaha" with a fatha on the zay. According to Ibn 'Atiyyah, it is a verbal noun like az-zilzal with a kasra. Al-Zamakhshari said: the kasrah form is a verbal noun, and the fathah form is the name of the known motion, and it is used here in the accusative as a verbal noun by metonymy, since it occupies the place of the verbal noun. He also said:

There is no pattern fa'lal with a fatha in the forms (abniyah) except in the doubled (mudda'af) roots, and they mention that both fatha and kasra are permissible in that; however, the more common when it has a fatha is that it is in the sense of the active participle, like salsal meaning musalsal, qadqad meaning muqaqqad, and wiswas meaning muwaswis; according to Ibn Malik it is not a verbal noun. As for non-doubled forms, it is attested only rarely, whether as an adjective or a fixed noun; bahram and bastam are loanwords if the fatha in them is held to be correct. Among the rare forms is khaz'al with two dotted letters, meaning a she-camel with a limp, and some have not recorded any other. Tha'lab added qahqaz, meaning a hard stone; it was said to be a plural, and it was said to be a weak dialect, the eloquent form being qahqar with a doubled ra'. Another added qistal, meaning dust. This earthquake, according to a group who held this view, occurs at the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thaniyah), in accordance with the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 99, verse 2:

﴿And the earth will bring forth its burdens﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: that is, its dead. An-Naqqash, az-Zajjaj and Mundhir ibn Saʿid said: that is, its treasures and its dead. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: these treasures, according to this opinion, are other than the treasures that will come out in the days of the Dajjal (the Antichrist), as the reports have related; this is by bringing forth some of them in his days and some at the second blast (al-nafkha al-thaniya). There is no improbability in there being treasures after the Dajjal as well, which it will bring forth together with what remained that day. It has also been said: it occurs at the first blast, and its burdens are what is in its belly of treasures, or of treasures and of the dead, and the time is considered to be extended. It has been said: it is possible that the bringing forth of the dead, like the treasures, occurs at the first blast, and their revival at the second blast, and that they will be upon the surface of the earth between the two blasts; but you know that this contradicts what the texts indicate. It has also been said: it will be shaken at the first blast so it brings forth its treasures, and it will be shaken at the second so it brings forth its dead. Here, by the time of the quaking is meant what encompasses both times. Some restricted the interpretation of the burdens to treasures while the intended time is the time of the second blast, and said: the earth will bring forth its treasures on the Day of Resurrection so that the people of the standing place (al-mawqif) may see them, and the disobedient will be filled with regret when they look at them, for the places where they disobeyed God, Exalted is He, regarding them, and then they will leave them, while they avail them nothing.

In the hadith: "The earth will cast forth the fillets of its liver, like pillars of gold and silver. The murderer will come and say: 'For this I killed.' The one who severed kinship will come and say: 'For this I severed my kinship.' The thief will come and say: 'For this my hand was cut off.' Then they will leave it, and they will take nothing from it." It has also been said that this is so that with them will be branded the foreheads, sides and backs of those who hoarded.

Whatever the case, al-athqal (the burdens) is the plural of thiql (with a fatha on the thaʾ and a sukun on the qaf... the vowelled form being thiql with kasra and sukun, or thaql with fatha and sukun per the lexicon), which according to the Qamus is the goods of a traveller and every precious thing that is guarded; and it is used here figuratively for the second. It is also possible that it is the plural of thiql (with a kasra and sukun), meaning the burden of the belly, by way of simile and metaphor too, as ash-Sharif al-Murtada said in ad-Durar; and he indicated that it is not applied to what has been mentioned except by way of metaphor. Some interpreted al-athqal here as the secrets, but this, besides contradicting what is transmitted, is far-fetched. The manifesting of "the earth" in the place of a pronoun is for the increase of emphasis; it has been said: to hint at the earth being changed into another earth, or because the bringing forth of the earth is the state of some of its parts. The apparent meaning is that its bringing forth of that is caused by the quaking, as a carpet is shaken out to expel the dust and the like from it; and the waw was preferred over the fa' to leave the listener's mind free (tafwidan li-dhihn al-samiʿ), so it is said. Perhaps the apparent meaning is that causation and being caused were not intended, but rather each of the events mentioned is named without any indication that one is caused by another.

﴿And man says﴾, i.e., every single individual of mankind, because of what overwhelms them of the all-encompassing catastrophe and what sweeps over them of the general calamity: ﴿"What is the matter with it?"﴾ And this stage of quaking has been shaken with a violent quake, and it has brought out its burdens, in amazement at what they witnessed of the awe-inspiring event. The mountains have been set moving through the air and turned into scattered dust. Some have held that by "man" is meant the disbeliever who denies the resurrection (al-ba'th), but the more apparent view is the first, on the basis that the believer says this by way of amazement (al-istiʿzam) and the disbeliever by way of wonder (al-taʿajjub).

﴿Yawma'idhin﴾ (On that Day) is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for *idhā* (when). His saying, ﴿tuḥaddithu akhbārahā﴾ (it will relate its news), means that *al-arḍ* (the earth) is the subject. The possibility, as al-Ṭabarsī claimed, that the subject is the addressee has no basis, since it is the governing element (*'āmil*) for both of them.

It was also said that the governing element is an implied verb, indicated by the meaning of the clauses that follow, and the implied meaning is: "They will be gathered when it is shaken."

﴿Yawma'idhin﴾ is connected to ﴿tuḥaddithu﴾, and *idhā* is connected to it merely to indicate time (*ẓarfiyyah*). It was also said that it is in the accusative as the object of an implied *"udhkur"* (remember), meaning "remember that time," so it is neither a time adverb nor a conditional. It was permitted that it be a conditional (*sharṭiyyah*) governed by an implied response, meaning: "That which its true nature cannot be grasped, or the like, will occur." The intended meaning is: on the Day when it is shaken with its shaking, and it brings out its burdens, and man says, "What is wrong with it?", it will relate to creation the news it holds. This happens when Allah creates in it life and perception, and it speaks in reality, so it bears witness to what was done upon it of obedience or disobedience. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Thawri and others. The hadith that is ḥasan, ṣaḥīḥ, gharīb supports it.

Imam Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿On that Day it will relate its news﴾. Then he said: 'Do you know what its news is?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'Its news is that it will bear witness against every servant, male and female, to what they did upon its surface. It will say: "He did such-and-such on such-and-such a day." This is its news.'"

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, commentary on surah 99, verse 5:

The *bāʼ* (ب) in His, the Exalted's, words ﴿because your Lord has inspired it﴾ is causal (*lil-sababiyya*, expressing cause). The meaning is: it will relate its news because of your Lord's inspiring it and His, glorified is He, commanding it to relate. The *lām* (ل) in *lahā* carries the sense of *ilā* (to). That is, He inspired to it, because the familiar construction for *al-waḥy* (inspiration) is to govern it with *bi-hā* (with), as in His, the Exalted's, words ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾. However, it may also be governed by *lām*, as in the words of al-ʿAjjāj describing the earth:

*He inspired to it its settling, so it settled, and fastened it with the firm, established mountains.*

Perhaps the choice of this construction is for the sake of matching the verse-endings (*fawāṣil*). It is also permitted that the *lām* be for causation or benefit (*lil-taʿlīl aw al-manfaʿa*), because by the earth relating the deeds of the disobedient, it obtains a kind of satisfaction against them by exposing them and mentioning their ugly deeds, and it is also the one inspired. Inspiration may be inspiration of *ilhām* (inner inspiration), or inspiration of *irsāl* (sending), by which He, glorified is He, sends to it a messenger from the angels with that. Al-Tabari and a group said:

The "relating" is a metaphor (*istiʿāra*) or an unrestricted metonymy (*majāz mursal*) for the general indication of its state. The "inspiring" is the bringing about of that by which it indicates, so that He, mighty and majestic, brings about in it states that become an indication standing in place of relating with the tongue, until the one who says "What is wrong with it?" looks at those states, and knows why it was shaken and why it expelled the dead. This is what the prophets, peace be upon them, used to warn of and caution against, and it is not what they know of its news.

It was said: the inspiring, on the supposition that the relating is literal too, is also a metaphor for bringing about a state in which He, glorified is He, makes it speak, like the bringing into existence of life, the power of speech, and informing, as you have just heard. Yaḥyā ibn Sallām said: it relates what it brought out of its burdens. What supports this is what is in the *Hadith* of Ibn Mājah in his *Sunan*: "The earth will say on the Day of Resurrection: O Lord, this is what You entrusted to me."

From Ibn Masʿūd: it relates the establishment of the Hour when a person says, "What is wrong with it?" Then it informs that the affair of the world has ended and the affair of the Hereafter has come, so that will be an answer to them when they ask.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permitted that the meaning be: it relates by a relating of "that your Lord inspired it" its news, such that its relating that your Lord inspired it is a relating by its informing, just as you say: "You advised me every advice," meaning, "You advised me in religion." So its news is upon this that your Lord inspired it. The *bāʼ* is *tajrīdiyya* (of abstraction, the *bāʼ* that makes the thing relating itself), like its usage in your saying: "If you meet so-and-so, you will surely meet with him a man who is extremely good."

The apparent reading would be: "it relates its news" in the singular, and likewise according to the two options before it. But it has been put in the plural for emphasis, as the example and similar usage indicate, such as the poet's words:

*He granted me every wish with a visit that was a stolen glance, like the swoop of a bird.*

*If you could, you would have spread out the darkness to lengthen our night, O blackness of the pupil.*

Its remoteness is not hidden. Abū Ḥayyān went to great lengths in disparaging it, saying: "It is *ʿafsh* (trash), from which the Qur'an should be free." By *ʿafsh*, with an unpointed *ʿayn*, *fāʾ*, and a pointed *shīn*, he meant what defiles a dwelling of sweepings. It is a word that the common people of the Maghrib use for this, and it is not as he said.

It is also permitted that "that your Lord..." and so on be a substitute (*badal*) for "its news", as if it were said: "On that day it will relate that your Lord inspired it," because you say: "I related to him such-and-such" and "I related to him with such-and-such." So it is valid to substitute "that..." etc. for "its news", and one of them is genitive and the other accusative, because the substitute takes the place of the other in some usages. This is not impossible, contrary to Abū Ḥayyān, as in "I sought forgiveness for the great sin" with the accusative *al-dhanb* and the genitive *al-ʿaẓīm*, taking *al-ʿaẓīm* as an adjective (*naʿt*) of it with regard to the expression "I sought forgiveness from the sin." Because the substitute is the intended element, it has the force of another governing element, unlike the adjective. Yes, this too is contrary to the apparent meaning. And after all this, the proper course is not to depart from what has been transmitted, especially when it is authentically related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

[p. 211]

A discussion remains here: they differed concerning expressions like "I was related to" (*ḥuddithtu*): is it transitive to one object or to more? Al-Zamakhshari and others, and it is transmitted from Sībawayh, held that it is transitive to more. In their view it is assimilated to verbs of the heart (*afʿāl al-qulūb*), so it governs two objects, like "I related the news to Zayd," or three, like "I related him to ʿAmr standing." So "its news" is the second object, and the first object is omitted, as we have pointed out, and it was not mentioned because mentioning it serves no purpose, since the purpose is to make the day terrifying, and that it is among the days on which inanimate things speak, regardless of who the one relating is.

Shaykh Ibn al-Ḥājib said: it is only transitive to one object, and what comes after it is because the absolute object (*al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq*) is determined. "ʿAmran qāʾiman" in "I related to Zayd ʿAmran qāʾiman" is accusative because it occupies the place of the verbal noun (*maṣdar*), not because it is a second or third object. It is not said: how can what is not a verb in meaning occupy the position of a verbal noun, namely "ʿAmran qāʾiman" as a verbal noun? It was not a verbal noun in terms of being "ʿAmr standing," but in terms of being a particular speech (*ḥadīth*). The aspect that validated predicating it of the speech when you say "The speech of Zayd: ʿAmr is standing" is the same that validated its occurrence as a verbal noun. So "its news" here is in the position of the object, and the object is omitted for what has preceded. Rather, some of them said: if you say "I related to him a speech (*ḥadīth*) or a news (*khabar*)," there is no dispute that it is an absolute object, and it is apparent that "news" (*al-ikhbār*) in his view is likewise. This was challenged in *al-Kashf* by saying that what the Shaykh mentioned is not accepted, for he did not distinguish between *al-taḥdīth* (relating) and *al-ḥadīth* (speech). The former is the absolute object, how so, when it is governed by *bāʼ*, so you say: "I related to him the news" and "with the news." It is known that what the *bāʼ* governs cannot be an absolute object. It may be said: the Shaykh's not distinguishing is within the scope of prohibition, and how could such a thing be hidden from one of his standing? But he holds that the effect of the verbal noun and its complement has filled its place in what has been mentioned, just as its instrument fills its place in expressions like "I struck him with a whip." Perhaps what he established applies to cases other than those governed by *bāʼ*. Al-Ṭībī said: it is possible to say that *ḥaddatha* and its sisters are transitive to one object literally, and making them transitive to three or two is a figurative extension (*tajawwuz*) or an implicit meaning (*taḍmīn*) of the sense of informing. He found support for this in a passage he transmitted from *al-Mufaṣṣal* and a passage he transmitted from the author of *al-Iqlīd*, so reflect.

Ibn Masʿūd read: "it will inform of its news" (*tunabbiʾu akhbārahā*). Saʿīd ibn Jubayr read: "tunbiʾu" with the light form (*bi-l-takhfīf*).

﴿On that Day﴾ means: on the day that has been mentioned. It (yawma'idhin) is an adverb of time governing His saying, exalted is He: ﴿people will come forth﴾, that is, they will come out of their graves after they had been buried in them, toward the place of reckoning, ﴿in scattered groups﴾, dispersed according to their classes. Some will have white faces, secure, and some will have black faces, fearful; some will be riding and some walking; some will be shackled with chains and some not shackled.

It is reported from some of the early generations (al-salaf): dispersed toward the fortunate and the most fortunate, and toward the wretched and the most wretched.

It was also said: toward the believer and the disbeliever. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the people of faith will be apart, and the people of each religion will be apart. It is also permissible that what is meant is that each one will be alone, with no helper and no supporter, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾. It was also said: dispersed according to regions.

﴿That they may be shown their deeds﴾ means: that they may see the recompense of their deeds, whether good or evil. Thus the seeing is visual (ru'ya basriyya). The statement either contains an elision (of a modifier, i.e., "the records of their deeds") or uses "deeds" figuratively for what results from them of recompense. Some scholars supplied "books" or "scrolls." Another said: there is no need for interpretation (ta'wil, figurative reading), and deeds are embodied as luminous and dark forms; it is permissible to see them even though they are accidents. But that, as you see, is not so.

It was also said: what is meant is that they may know their deeds and be made to stand over them in detail at the reckoning, so that there is no need for what was mentioned as well. Al-Naqqash said: "al-sudur" (issuing forth) is the opposite of "al-wurud" (arriving), so they come to the gathering place and depart from it dispersed: some to Paradise and some to the Fire, ﴿that they may be shown﴾ the recompense of their deeds, of Paradise and Fire. But this is not the correct view.

Whatever the case, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that they may be shown﴾ is connected to ﴿will come forth﴾. It was also said that it is connected to ﴿Your Lord has inspired it﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD).

Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Qatada, Hammad ibn Salama, al-Zuhri, Abu Haywa, 'Isa, and Nafi' in one transmission read ﴿liyaraw﴾ (ليَرَوْا) with a fatha on the ya'.

صفحة 212

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ ﴿and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾. This is an elaboration of "they will be shown" (liyuraw). The *dharra* (speck, atom) is a small red, delicate ant. It is said that it moves when a year has passed over it, and it is a proverbial example of smallness.

Imru' al-Qays said:

*From the modest-gazed women, if a mhwl (a tiny creature) of the dharr crawled on the saddle-cloth of one of them, it would leave a mark.*

It is also said that *dharr* is what is seen in the rays of the sun, the floating dust. Hannad related from Ibn 'Abbas that he put his hand into the dust, then raised it and blew on it, and said: "Each one of these is a *mithqal dharra*."

The accusatives *khayran* and *sharran* are in the function of specification (tamyiz), because *mithqal dharra* is a measure. It is also said that they are in apposition (badal) to *mithqal*. The apparent meaning is that *man* in both places is general, covering the believer and the disbeliever, and that what is meant by seeing what equals an atom's weight of good or evil is witnessing its recompense, in that this comes to him. This has been challenged on the ground that this entails the disbeliever being rewarded for his good deeds, whereas they have said that the deeds of the disbelievers are nullified, and in Sharh al-Maqasid he claimed consensus on this. How is that so, when He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And We turn to whatever deeds they did, and make them scattered dust﴾, and the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire, and what they did there is nullified, and what they used to do is void﴾, and the Exalted says: ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes﴾ and so on... And that the good they see is a lightening of the punishment is refuted by His saying: ﴿So the punishment will not be lightened for them﴾, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿We will increase them in punishment upon punishment, because of what they used to corrupt﴾. It also entails the punishment of a believer for his minor sins when he avoids the major sins, whereas they have said that these are expiated in that case, because of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will expiate from you your misdeeds﴾. And Ibn al-Munayyir's statement that avoidance does not necessitate expiation according to the majority, but rather repentance or the will of Allah the Exalted, is worthless, because repentance and avoidance are equal in the ruling of the text, and the will of Allah the Exalted is the original cause. So some have been compelled to hold that what is meant by "whoever" in the first clause is the happy ones, and in the second the wretched ones, on the basis that ﴿So whoever does﴾ and so on is an elaboration of ﴿men will come forth in scattered groups﴾, and this was explained with a meaning whose essence is: ﴿a group in the Garden and a group in the Blaze﴾. Therefore it is fitting that each clause return to one group, for the elaboration to correspond to what was summarized. Also, the apparent sense of His, glorified is He, "So whoever does, and whoever does," with the repetition of the conditional particle, requires difference between the two doers.

Others said it is general, but some of them said: there is an implied restriction in the statement, left out for its clarity and because it is known from other verses. The estimate is: "So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, if it is not nullified. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, if it is not expiated." Some of them made the seeing more general, covering what happens in this world and what happens in the Hereafter. So the disbeliever sees the recompense of his good in this world and the recompense of his evil in the Hereafter, and the believer sees the recompense of his evil in this world and the recompense of his good in the Hereafter. Al-Baghawi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that he said: "So whoever does an atom's weight of good while he is a disbeliever, he will see the reward of that in this world, in himself, his family and his wealth, until he reaches the Hereafter, and there will be no good for him in it. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil while he is a believer, it will be repaid to him in this world, in himself, his family and his wealth, until he reaches the Hereafter, and there will be no evil for him in it."

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, Ibn Abi Hatim and a group related from Anas, who said: "While Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, was eating with the Prophet (ﷺ), there was revealed to him: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight﴾ and so on. Abu Bakr raised his hand and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, am I going to see every atom's weight of evil I have done?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Abu Bakr, do you see what you see in this world of what you dislike? It is the atoms' weights of evil, and there is stored up for you the atoms' weights of good until He pays them to you on the Day of Resurrection.'"

In the narration of Ibn Mardawayh from Abu Ayyub, when he raised his hand, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Whoever among you does good, its reward is in the Hereafter, and whoever among you does evil, he will see it in this world as afflictions and sicknesses, and whoever has in him an atom's weight of good enters the Garden."

Some said: what is meant by seeing what equals that of good and evil is witnessing the self itself, without taking into account the recompense or its absence. Rather, each of them is left to the other proofs that speak of the pardoning of the believer's minor sins when he avoids the major sins, and of the confirmation of all his good deeds, and of the nullification of the disbeliever's good deeds and his punishment for all his sins. And this is indicated by what Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning his statement on the verse: "There is no believer or disbeliever who has done good and evil in

صفحة 213

this world except that Allah the Exalted shows it to him. As for the believer, he sees his good deeds and his misdeeds, so He forgives him of his misdeeds and rewards him for his good deeds. As for the disbeliever, He shows him his good deeds and his misdeeds, so He rejects his good deeds and punishes him for his misdeeds."

Al-Tibi chose this and said: "It is supported by the composition, the meaning and the style. As for the composition, His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So whoever does﴾ and so on is an elaboration of what was followed by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿men will come forth in scattered groups, to be shown their deeds﴾, so there must be correspondence. The deeds (a'mal) is a plural noun with a possessive suffix, which conveys totality and comprehensiveness. 'Men will come forth' is restricted by His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿in scattered groups﴾, which means they are on various paths toward alighting in their stations of the Garden and the Fire according to their differing deeds. For this reason the Garden has degrees and the Fire has levels. صفحة 212

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ ﴿and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾. This is an elaboration of "they will be shown" (liyuraw). The *dharra* (speck, atom) is a small red, delicate ant. It is said that it moves when a year has passed over it, and it is a proverbial example of smallness.

Imru' al-Qays said:

*From the modest-gazed women, if a mhwl (a tiny creature) of the dharr crawled on the saddle-cloth of one of them, it would leave a mark.*

It is also said that *dharr* is what is seen in the rays of the sun, the floating dust. Hannad related from Ibn 'Abbas that he put his hand into the dust, then raised it and blew on it, and said: "Each one of these is a *mithqal dharra*."

The accusatives *khayran* and *sharran* are in the function of specification (tamyiz), because *mithqal dharra* is a measure. It is also said that they are in apposition (badal) to *mithqal*. The apparent meaning is that *man* in both places is general, covering the believer and the disbeliever, and that what is meant by seeing what equals an atom's weight of good or evil is witnessing its recompense, in that this comes to him. This has been challenged on the ground that this entails the disbeliever being rewarded for his good deeds, whereas they have said that the deeds of the disbelievers are nullified, and in Sharh al-Maqasid he claimed consensus on this. How is that so, when He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And We turn to whatever deeds they did, and make them scattered dust﴾, and the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire, and what they did there is nullified, and what they used to do is void﴾, and the Exalted says: ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes﴾ and so on... And that the good they see is a lightening of the punishment is refuted by His saying: ﴿So the punishment will not be lightened for them﴾, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿We will increase them in punishment upon punishment, because of what they used to corrupt﴾. It also entails the punishment of a believer for his minor sins when he avoids the major sins, whereas they have said that these are expiated in that case, because of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will expiate from you your misdeeds﴾. And Ibn al-Munayyir's statement that avoidance does not necessitate expiation according to the majority, but rather repentance or the will of Allah the Exalted, is worthless, because repentance and avoidance are equal in the ruling of the text, and the will of Allah the Exalted is the original cause. So some have been compelled to hold that what is meant by "whoever" in the first clause is the happy ones, and in the second the wretched ones, on the basis that ﴿So whoever does﴾ and so on is an elaboration of ﴿men will come forth in scattered groups﴾, and this was explained with a meaning whose essence is: ﴿a group in the Garden and a group in the Blaze﴾. Therefore it is fitting that each clause return to one group, for the elaboration to correspond to what was summarized. Also, the apparent sense of His, glorified is He, "So whoever does, and whoever does," with the repetition of the conditional particle, requires difference between the two doers.

Others said it is general, but some of them said: there is an implied restriction in the statement, left out for its clarity and because it is known from other verses. The estimate is: "So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, if it is not nullified. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, if it is not expiated." Some of them made the seeing more general, covering what happens in this world and what happens in the Hereafter. So the disbeliever sees the recompense of his good in this world and the recompense of his evil in the Hereafter, and the believer sees the recompense of his evil in this world and the recompense of his good in the Hereafter. Al-Baghawi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that he said: "So whoever does an atom's weight of good while he is a disbeliever, he will see the reward of that in this world, in himself, his family and his wealth, until he reaches the Hereafter, and there will be no good for him in it.
